issues.legal_issue: A coparcener’s clear communication of an intention to separate can sever Mitakshara joint-family status even when a subsequent written allotment is described as being for maintenance.
material_facts: The brothers belonged to an undivided Mitakshara joint family, and the family property was not subject to a proved custom of impartibility or primogeniture.

The deed recited that one brother had recently desired to live separately after division and permanently allotted identified lands to him and his male descendants, without reserving a right of reversion.
The brother held and enjoyed the allotted lands exclusively for decades, with revenue records in his name.
After abolition of the watan system, he alone sought regrant of the allotted lands; the other family members knew of this and did not object, while they sought regrant of other lands without him.
issues.conclusion: The brothers’ joint-family status had been severed before the deed was executed, and the lands allotted by the deed were the separate property of the brother who received them.
issues.legal_principle: Under Mitakshara Hindu law, partition includes severance of joint status and does not require an immediate division of property by metes and bounds. A coparcener can cause severance by clearly communicating an intention to separate and enjoy his share separately; the communication and its effect may be inferred from the document, surrounding circumstances, and subsequent conduct. Once severance occurs, it cannot be undone by mere withdrawal of the communication, absent reunion. The Court relied on Appavier v. Rama Subha Aiyan, Giria Bai v. Sadashiv, Bhagwan Dayal v. Mst. Reoti Devi, Puttorangamma v. Ranganna, and the principles stated in Mulla’s and Mayne’s Hindu Law.

rule.if: civil_property_appeal and mitakshara_joint_family_existed and clear_separation_intimation and permanent_exclusive_allocation and subsequent_separate_dealings

predicates.civil_property_appeal: The proceeding is a civil appeal concerning competing claims to ownership and possession of family property.
predicates.mitakshara_joint_family_existed: The property holders belonged to an undivided family governed by Mitakshara law.
predicates.clear_separation_intimation: A coparcener communicated to another coparcener a clear intention to separate and enjoy his share independently.
predicates.permanent_exclusive_allocation: A family member permanently allocated identified property to the coparcener for his exclusive enjoyment without reserving a right of reversion.
predicates.subsequent_separate_dealings: The recipient and the other family members later dealt with the allocated and remaining property separately.

issues.definition: When an undivided Mitakshara family member clearly communicates an intention to separate, receives a permanent exclusive allocation, and the family thereafter deals with the property separately in a civil property appeal, the joint status is severed and the allotted property is separate.

issues.legal_issue: The rule against using extrinsic evidence to vary written terms does not bar evidence concerning a preliminary recital of past fact or evidence showing that a writing’s apparent character does not reflect the real transaction.
material_facts: The deed contained a preliminary recital describing a prior request to live separately after division, as well as operative provisions allocating land.
The dispute concerned whether the recital and the deed’s maintenance terminology reflected the actual transaction and whether the family’s joint status had already been severed.
The Court used the recital, surrounding circumstances, and subsequent conduct to determine the deed’s true character without varying its operative terms.
issues.conclusion: The evidentiary bar did not prevent consideration of extrinsic evidence concerning the preliminary recital or the true character of the transaction.
issues.legal_principle: Section 92 of the Evidence Act bars evidence that varies, contradicts, adds to, or subtracts from the terms of a written disposition, but does not bar evidence concerning a preliminary recital of past fact that is not itself a dispositive term. Evidence de hors the document may also be led where the dispute concerns whether the writing is an illusory or colourable device that cloaks the real transaction. The Court relied on Chandi Prasad Singh v. Piari Bidi and Bhagwan Dayal v. Mst. Reoti Devi.

predicates.civil_property_appeal: The proceeding is a civil appeal concerning competing claims to property.
predicates.disputed_writing_exists: The parties dispute the meaning or character of a written transaction.
predicates.writing_contains_preliminary_past_fact_r: The writing includes a preliminary account of an event or communication that occurred before the writing was made.
predicates.extrinsic_evidence_tests_recital_or_true: A party offers evidence from outside the writing to test the truth of the preliminary recital or the writing’s apparent character.
predicates.extrinsic_evidence_varies_dispositive_te: The offered evidence would contradict, vary, add to, or subtract from the writing’s operative disposition of property.

issues.definition: In a civil property appeal, extrinsic evidence may be considered to test a preliminary recital or the true character of a writing if the evidence does not vary its operative terms.

issues.legal_issue: Under traditional Hindu law, a daughter succeeds to her father’s separate property in preference to collateral family members.
material_facts: The Court found that the lands were the deceased father’s separate property when he died.
His daughter claimed the lands, while the plaintiffs claimed as collateral family members.
issues.conclusion: The daughter inherited the separate property to the exclusion of the collateral claimants.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied traditional Hindu law of succession, under which the daughter succeeds to her father’s separate estate in preference to the collateral claimants in this case. The Court did not rely on a statutory provision or an earlier case for this conclusion.

predicates.separate_estate_succession_dispute: The proceeding involves competing succession claims to a deceased parent’s property.
predicates.property_was_deceased_parent_separate_pr: The property belonged separately to the deceased parent when the parent died.
predicates.deceased_parent_left_daughter: The deceased parent left a daughter who claims the property.
predicates.collateral_relatives_claimed_as_successo: Relatives who are collateral to the deceased parent also claim the property as successors.

issues.definition: When a daughter and collateral relatives dispute succession to a deceased parent’s separate property, the daughter inherits in preference to the collateral relatives.
